I will keep my land in the usual North China Plain double-cropping pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize. In Quzhou County, that is the system I trust most because it fits the local climate, my experience, the irrigation conditions, and the machinery I can manage at my age. I would not spread myself across too many crops. I want stable output, straightforward field operations, and lower risk. Winter wheat is already the backbone of my spring field management, and after harvest I will turn the same land quickly into summer maize so I can use the full year efficiently.

For wheat, I will focus on water and fertilizer timing instead of chasing very high input. At the start of the season, my main job is to protect tiller survival, support stem elongation, and prevent lodging and disease. I will use improved wheat seed types that are locally adapted, keep nitrogen moderate, add phosphorus and potassium for root strength and grain filling, and irrigate at the critical stages rather than too often. I will spray only when disease or aphid pressure justifies it. After wheat harvest, I will move fast into summer maize with hybrid seed. Maize gives me reliable yield in this rotation, and hybrid seed is worth it for stand uniformity and production. I will keep fertilizer balanced, use fewer irrigations than wheat unless drought forces more, and manage weeds and insects with a small number of targeted pesticide applications. For tillage, I will use rotary tillage before maize because it fits my equipment and lets me prepare the seedbed quickly after wheat harvest.
